These potential scenarios were narrowed to 79 unique outcomes, where the majority were classified as low or medium risk, with only one scenario reaching the high-risk threshold. The 79 unique scenarios were simplified further into categories of “higher” and “lower” risk. The highest-rated risk identified in the analysis involves catastrophic tank failure or a boiling liquid expanding vapor explosion (BLEVE). These events may be caused by extreme external impacts, such as seismic events or collisions, or the failure of safety devices such as temperature and pressure relief devices (TPRDs) or rupture discs. Medium-risk scenarios are primarily driven by thermal/pressure deviations or human factors. Improper indoor defueling, such as opening manual valves without a venting tool (note: venting tool is described in Section 2.2), and hot work operations such as welding or grinding near hydrogen leak sources pose possible threats of unintended ignition or system overpressurization. Many hazardous scenarios identified in this analysis require the simultaneous occurrence of multiple failures, such as a component malfunction happening as well as a human error or the absence of a safety barrier. Because these systems are designed with multiple redundancies, including automatic shutoff valves, leak detection sensors, and TPRDs/rupture discs, a single point of failure is typically insufficient to cause a catastrophic event. These built-in failsafes ensure that even if a deviation occurs, the hydrogen is either contained or safely managed, keeping the frequency of a high-severity incident as low as possible. Hydrogen rail cars introduce different maintenance risks that may require specialized consideration. Therefore, to ensure the safe integration of hydrogen rail into maintenance infrastructure, several critical preventative and mitigative measures can be considered. Rail cars should ideally be defueled before entering the facility, but if indoor defueling is required, the verification of the proper connection of a venting tool and vent stacks is important to ensure hydrogen is vented to the outside. Facility design approaches that can mitigate hydrogen hazards include maintenance pits and ceilings that are unobstructed and well-ventilated, roof structures capable of venting hydrogen, and rails mounted on posts to reduce maintenance pit enclosure where hydrogen can accumulate.
